title: The Broken Spire
premise: Marguerite Thornbury, a bone-carver who hears the dead through the relics she carves, lives in the Valley of Vell, a pocket of the world where magic cannot follow and where the vanished country of Osterhale supposedly died a century ago. When a prophecy book written in 1823 names her and tonight's date, Marguerite learns that Osterhale never fell—it was folded out of existence by its own Spire-wardens, who traded memory for power, and the valley is the prison they built to hold the witnesses. Guided by the voice of a dead cartographer lodged in an old femur, Marguerite must find the Door Out before the wardens finish erasing the valley's memories one household at a time. In the end, she chooses truth over loyalty: she shatters the Spire's heart-bone, restoring Osterhale at the cost of her own gift—and her place in the world's memory—so that everyone else can finally be remembered.
about_author: H. M. Ashgrove is the pen name of a former museum conservator who spent a decade cataloguing Victorian bone carvings before turning to fiction. They write from a farmhouse in the Pennines, where they keep an unexplained collection of antique keys.

chapters.title: The Date That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. While carving a commission from a client's grandmother's rib, Marguerite hears the dead woman hum a tune—and finds today's date inked in a water-damaged prophecy book bought at market. The beat is quiet dread: the ordinary life of the valley cracks open on an otherwise unremarkable evening.

chapters.title: What the Bone Remembers
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Following the humming, Marguerite excavates a hidden cache beneath the workshop floor: a femur belonging to Edric Vale, a cartographer dead a century, whose voice insists he was murdered for drawing a map of a door. The emotional beat is reluctant wonder—Marguerite has always heard the dead, but never been heard back.

chapters.title: The Valley That Keeps Its Mouth Shut
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Asking neighbors about Osterhale, Marguerite hits a wall of cheerful blankness; even the parish records end mid-sentence in 1823. Aunt Sable warns them to burn the book. The beat is isolation sharpening into resolve—the first hint that forgetting here is not natural but enforced.

chapters.title: A Visitor Without Footprints
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A courteous stranger called Warden Corvane arrives, ostensibly appraising antiques, and asks precise questions about the prophecy book. He leaves no footprints in the fresh snow. The beat is cold fear: power has noticed the valley's one loose thread, and it is polite about it.

chapters.title: Edric's Map
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, with Edric's voice threading through. Working nights, Marguerite carves the femur's marrow-canal open and reads the map etched inside bone: the Door Out lies beneath the drowned chapel past the ridge—but the ridge, by every map, does not exist. The beat is obsession taking root.

chapters.title: The First Household to Forget
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The Weaver family wakes unable to recall their youngest son, though his bed is still warm. Marguerite alone remembers him, because the boy once gave her a tooth to carve. The beat is grief and guilt—Marguerite realizes the erasure began the night they opened the book.

chapters.title: Sable's Confession
chapters.summary: Aunt Sable's POV. Sable reveals she was born outside the valley, a Spire archivist who fled with a stolen page of the prophecy book and paid for it with her sister's memory of her. She begs Marguerite to stop. The beat is betrayal braided with love—loyalty demanding silence while truth demands action.

chapters.title: Over the Ridge That Isn't There
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Carrying Edric's femur as compass, Marguerite climbs at night and steps through a fold in the mist onto land that aches with absence: ruined roads, orchards turned to ash-shapes, the drowned chapel's bell tower breaking the water. The beat is awe curdling into horror at the scale of what was taken.

chapters.title: The Drowned Chapel
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Diving into the chapel, Marguerite finds the Door Out—a bone-white archway sealed with seven locks, each keyed to a memory freely given. Edric confesses his lock was his name, surrendered before he died trying to warn the valley. The beat is despair at a price Marguerite isn't sure they can pay.

chapters.title: Corvane's Offer
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Corvane intercepts Marguerite at the water's edge and offers a bargain: walk away, and the valley keeps its small happinesses; open the Door, and every erased soul returns—but so do the wardens' crimes, and the valley will remember its complicity. The beat is temptation framed as mercy.

chapters.title: The Tooth
chapters.summary: The forgotten boy's POV, brief and luminous. Existing between memory and erasure, the boy clings to the carved tooth Marguerite made him and pushes against the forgetting, reaching toward anyone who might still say his name. The beat is fragile hope—the proof that love outlasts enforced oblivion.

chapters.title: Locks One Through Three
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. At the Door, Marguerite gives three memories freely: their mother's lullaby, the smell of the workshop, the first time they heard the dead. Each lock opens; each loss hollows. The beat is sacrifice made tactile—power's opposite revealed as willing surrender.

chapters.title: Sable at the Threshold
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sable arrives to stop Marguerite and instead gives her fourth memory—her sister's face—to the lock, choosing truth over the loyalty that kept her silent for sixty years. The beat is redemption earned late, and the two women crossing a line neither can return over.

chapters.title: The Spire Wakes
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The remaining locks flare; across the valley, the Spire—a black needle no one had ever quite seen before—becomes visible on the horizon, and Corvane begins pulling memories wholesale, streets going blank behind him. The beat is the ticking clock made flesh: time is running out in the most literal way.

chapters.title: Edric's Last Secret
chapters.summary: Edric's voice, anchored in the femur, carries the chapter. He reveals the seventh lock needs a memory of the future—a thing only the living can give—and that he stayed dead on purpose so someone with Marguerite's gift would eventually hear him. The beat is devastating tenderness: a century-long act of faith in a stranger.

chapters.title: The Emptying
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs in fragments. The valley forgets in waves—names, faces, the word for bread—as Corvane harvests memory to feed the Spire. Marguerite, half-erased themselves, crawls toward the Door holding the boy's tooth. The beat is apocalyptic intimacy: the apocalypse measured in lost breakfasts and unlatched gates.

chapters.title: Locks Five and Six
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Half-blinded by erasure, Marguerite gives the sound of Edric's voice and the feeling of being believed. The Door stands one lock from opening, and Corvane arrives with Sable's emptied body beside him as leverage. The beat is rage refined into clarity—grief without illusion.

chapters.title: The Seventh Lock
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Facing Corvane, Marguerite speaks the memory of the future: a valley that remembers, a boy with his name back, a world with Osterhale in it again. The lock opens; Corvane falters, because he too was once a witness who chose power instead. The beat is the climax's hinge—truth offered even to the enemy.

chapters.title: The Heart-Bone
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Inside the Door lies the Spire's heart-bone, the relic holding the wardens' stolen centuries. To restore Osterhale, it must shatter—and Marguerite's gift, born of the same magic, will shatter with it. The beat is the final choice: keep the hearing that made them who they are, or give the world back its memory.

chapters.title: Shatter
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Marguerite breaks the heart-bone. Light floods the valley; the Spire crumbles; Corvane ages into dust whispering thank you; the dead fall silent in Marguerite's hands forever. The beat is triumphant loss—the loudest silence of Marguerite's life.

chapters.title: Osterhale, Remembered
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Osterhale unfolds back into the world: roads reconnect, the boy runs to the Weavers calling his own name, Sable's sister greets her at the border, and maps redraw themselves overnight. Marguerite watches, remembered by everyone except, perhaps, themselves. The beat is communal joy shadowed by private cost.

chapters.title: The Carver Who Hears Nothing
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Months later, Marguerite carves bone that says nothing back, content in a valley that now sits openly on every map. On the doorstep, a package: Edric's femur, polished smooth, with a new inscription—thank you—and, faintly, impossibly, one last hummed note. The beat is quiet grace: some doors, once opened, stay ajar.
